job.style: a step-by-step explanation of a process

passage: When you kick a football, you apply a force to it, but the ball does not contain any force within itself. Once your foot loses contact, the ball continues to move because of its inertia, not because of a force pushing it forward. If the ball is resting on the grass, it is not free of forces; gravity pulls it down, and the ground exerts an equal upward normal force, keeping it stationary. When the ball hits a wall, the wall exerts a force on the ball, and simultaneously, the ball exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. These two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other out. Even if a heavy truck hits a small car, the force exerted by the truck on the car is exactly equal in magnitude to the force exerted by the car on the truck. Momentum is a measure of motion, defined as the product of mass and velocity, and it remains conserved in all collisions, even when objects stick together after impact. An object in motion will maintain its velocity unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force, meaning a constant force is not required to keep an object moving at a constant speed.

items.evidence: Once your foot loses contact, the ball continues to move because of its inertia, not because of a force pushing it forward.
items.q: After the ball leaves your foot, why does it keep moving forward?
options: Because of its inertia, with no forward push
Because the kick's force is stored inside it
Because inertia is a force pushing it ahead
Because a force must keep pushing it along
items.explain: Once the foot leaves, inertia keeps the ball moving; no force pushes it forward.

wrong.why: thinks force is carried inside the object
thinks motion needs a continuous force

items.evidence: If the ball is resting on the grass, it is not free of forces; gravity pulls it down, and the ground exerts an equal upward normal force, keeping it stationary.
items.q: A football lies still on the grass. Which forces are acting on it?
options: Gravity down and the ground pushing up
No forces, because it is not moving
Only gravity, since grass cannot push
Only the force left from the last kick
items.explain: Gravity pulls the resting ball down and the ground pushes up equally, so it stays still.

wrong.why: thinks resting objects have no forces
thinks the ground cannot exert a force
thinks force stays stored in the ball

items.evidence: These two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other out.
items.q: A ball and a wall push each other equally. Why don't these two forces cancel out?
options: They act on two different objects
The wall's force comes slightly later
The ball pushes harder than the wall
They both act together on the ball
items.explain: One force acts on the ball and the other on the wall, so they cannot cancel.

wrong.why: misses that the forces are equal
reverses the passage: thinks both act on one object

items.evidence: Even if a heavy truck hits a small car, the force exerted by the truck on the car is exactly equal in magnitude to the force exerted by the car on the truck.
items.q: A heavy truck crashes into a small car. How do their forces on each other compare?
options: The forces are exactly equal in size
The truck's force is larger, being heavier
The car's force is larger, being smaller
The truck's force is larger, having more momentum
items.explain: The truck's force on the car exactly equals the car's force on the truck.

wrong.why: thinks the heavier object pushes harder
over-corrects and thinks the smaller object pushes harder

items.evidence: Momentum is a measure of motion, defined as the product of mass and velocity, and it remains conserved in all collisions, even when objects stick together after impact.
items.q: Two trolleys collide and stick together. What happens to their total momentum?
options: It stays the same as before the collision
It is lost because they stuck together
It is used up as force in the crash
It doubles because their masses combine
items.explain: Momentum is conserved in all collisions, even when objects stick together.

wrong.why: thinks force or motion gets used up
adds masses but forgets velocity changes
